column3: Near-verbatim parallel: revelation is refused in favor of what was found among the ancestors.
Its parents and secure entry concern family protection, not inherited religious following.
The people explicitly justify worship by saying they found their fathers practicing it.
It closely repeats the summons to revealed guidance and the reply that ancestral practice is sufficient.
The immediately preceding verse exposes argument about God without knowledge, guidance, or illuminating scripture.
The defense rests directly on finding the fathers doing the same thing.
Ancestral custom is falsely elevated into divine command and confronted with the lack of knowledge.
Within the surah, diversion from God's path without knowledge leads to punishment, reinforcing the warning's outcome.
It names the sinners' error and blazing condition, the destination named at the end of the focus.
A command to believe what God revealed is met by selective acceptance of inherited revelation.
Fear of the unseen Lord and the Hour does not address ancestral imitation or Satan's call.
Inherited names lack divine warrant, while people follow conjecture despite guidance from their Lord.
The vanished objects of invocation show failed false worship but not the focus's ancestral defense.
It contrasts obedience to parents in false association with following the path of those who turn to God.
The people reject following one human and associate it with error and burning, without ancestral imitation.
What the Lord has sent down is dismissed as tales of the ancients.
Its severe punishment is adjacent in theme but does not explain the competing paths of the focus.
It identifies Satan as a rebellious pattern of allegiance, clarifying the hidden leader behind a corrupt path.
Those summoned to what God revealed and to the Messenger turn decisively away.
Ancestors are demanded as proof of resurrection rather than followed as religious authority.
A caller summons people toward a dreadful matter, echoing the focus's dangerous call without its agent or destination.
Better guidance is explicitly set against what people found their fathers following.
The same surah's creation signs and descent of water do not directly address following or ancestral authority.
The Messenger calls people to faith in their Lord, furnishing the positive divine call opposed in the focus.
It records fear that following guidance will bring worldly loss, another resistance to accepting guidance.
Divine knowledge of the Hour, rain, and hidden human futures does not clarify the focus's choice of guidance.
Satan's deceptive speech initiates the pattern of being drawn away from God's command.
The people of the blaze admit that listening and reasoning would have kept them from that fate.
Adam's forgotten covenant offers only a remote contrast to deliberate inherited following.
It identifies the Qur'an as a revelation from the Merciful but does not address the response of following.
Whoever takes Satan as patron is led by him to the punishment of the blaze.
Its refusal to hear recited verses reinforces rejection of revelation but not inherited practice itself.
The blessed sending down of a warning supplies the revealed source rejected in the focus.
The message is rejected as an attempt to turn people away from what they found their fathers upon.
A question about the penalty for lying has no material connection to guidance or ancestral following.
Following the Qur'an's recitation gives a disciplined positive sense of following.
It directly commands following what was sent down from the Lord rather than other authorities.
The next verse states the secure outcome of submitting oneself to God and doing good.
Following a means in a journey does not concern religious allegiance or authority.
Satan calls his party so that they become companions of the blaze, closely matching the focus's warning.
Painful punishment alone does not supply the focus's call, guide, or ancestral rationale.
It expressly forbids following Satan's steps and identifies their command toward indecency and wrong.
The realized promise and exchange between Paradise and Fire do not explain the preceding choice of guide.
Cosmic alternation and God's knowledge of deeds do not illuminate inherited following or Satanic invitation.
The mention of former fathers belongs to a resurrection objection, not an appeal to ancestral practice.
Satan beautifies prior communities' deeds and becomes their patron, explaining deceptive attachment to a path.
The brothers' appeal for a substitute in custody is unrelated to the focus's guidance contrast.
Hell is portrayed as calling those who turned away and accumulated, reinforcing the active pull toward ruin.
They follow what angers God and dislike what pleases Him, directly contrasting rival objects of following.
The refusal to seize anyone except the one in whose possession the item was found is unrelated.
It announces ruin in a blazing fire, sharing the warned destination but not its path of invitation.
The blazing fire is named as a punishment prepared for devils, supporting the focus's Satan-fire association.
Deviation concerning God's names is related to corrupt religious practice but not to ancestral following.
Calling on beings besides God exposes their lack of ownership, without the focus's ancestral argument.
The single Muslim household concerns rescue and belief, not guidance accepted or rejected through ancestry.
Abraham questions the images to which his father and people are devoted, opening the ancestral-idolatry setting.
Noah's public call supplies a general calling motif without the rival authorities of the focus.
Satan admits that he merely called people and they answered, directly clarifying responsibility within his invitation.
Abraham declares both the people and their fathers to be in manifest error.
The Qur'an's deliberate sending down supplies the revealed guidance that the focus tells people to follow.
Without God's grace people would have followed Satan, contrasting disciplined referral with Satanic following.
The perception of Joseph's scent from the departing caravan is unrelated to the focus's moral guidance.
The descent of water and emergence of plants do not clarify the rival calls or their outcomes.
Following the magicians is conditioned on apparent victory, not on inherited religion or revelation.
The extraction of believers from a town does not address the choice between guidance and ancestral custom.
The question whether idols hear when called tests the efficacy of false objects of invocation.
Abraham warns his father not to worship Satan because Satan is disobedient to the Merciful.
The stated rule of recompense for the found object has no interpretive link to the focus.
Entering a blazing fire shares the focus's terminal punishment but not the route that leads there.
Departure from God's command is punished by the blaze, though no Satanic call or ancestral defense appears.
The secure inhabitants call for fruit, a benign invocation that only contrasts with the focus's destructive call.
Criminals see the Fire, know they will meet it, and find no escape from it.
Taking powerless, uncomprehending intercessors besides God parallels reliance on unauthorized religious authorities.
Protection from Hell's punishment gives the positive contrast to the focus's destination of the blaze.
A demand to bring back the fathers misdirects the evidentiary burden of revealed signs and resurrection.
It commands following messengers who seek no payment and are rightly guided.
The absence of refuge apart from God conveys exclusive dependence but not the focus's invitation or ancestry.
Noah's continual calling is a general parallel to calling, without the focus's deceptive source.
It sharply contrasts following falsehood with following truth from the Lord.
Moses' discovery of a fire and search for guidance there does not bear on the focus's moral warning.
Those cursed by God find no helper, a distant consequence parallel without the focus's path of following.
The offer of a clear sign is too general to clarify ancestral imitation or Satan's call.
Invented religious distinctions are attributed to God while reason is displaced, matching the critique of inherited authority.
The garden owner's presumptions about the Hour and return do not address the focus's competing guidance.
The denial of coercive authority in a dialogue of blame lacks the focus's call or inherited rationale.
God's knowledge, mercy, and punishment do not specifically clarify the focus's contrast of paths.
Reflection on the Qur'an supplies an alternative to untested imitation, but no direct following contrast is stated.
Calling on God alone in distress exposes the unreliability of associated partners.
They claim to have found their fathers on a community and to be guided by their tracks.
Repeated calls for destruction express punishment after the fact, not Satan's invitation to it.
People hear lies and follow selective instructions, showing distorted reception of religious authority.
The Messenger states that he follows only what is revealed to him, the positive model of the focus's command.
Satan beautifies people's deeds, promises support, then abandons them when the crisis arrives.
Exclusive worship is rejected because it would mean leaving what the fathers worshipped.
The Qur'an's force and God's complete command concern revelation's authority but not ancestral imitation.
Responding to God's and the Messenger's life-giving call contrasts with the focus's ruinous summons.
The preservation of Noah's mention among later generations does not clarify following or false worship.
People demand a sign be sent down, while the response locates the unseen and its timing with God.
The desire to turn believers back to disbelief is a hostile redirection, without the focus's ancestral basis.
Association without any revealed authority is challenged, directly supporting the focus's appeal to what God sent down.
Polytheists invoke God's will and their fathers to defend association and prohibition without knowledge.
Inherited names for supposed deities are denied any divine authority, directly challenging ancestral religious claims.
Salih's people reject his call because it would require leaving what their fathers worshipped.
Shu'ayb's people frame his message as a demand to abandon what their fathers worshipped.
Those who associate partners appeal to divine will and to their fathers' practice instead of accepting the messengers' warning.
God commands that His guidance be followed and makes that following the condition against going astray.
Abraham condemns worship of things that neither benefit nor harm, exposing the emptiness of inherited idolatry.
A person disputes about God without knowledge while following every rebellious Satan.
Turning arrogantly away from revelation leads others from God's path and toward the Fire.
The elites resist a messenger by portraying him as an ordinary man seeking superiority over inherited social authority.
Arrogant rejection and hostile talk about the revelation extend the focus's refusal to heed divine guidance.
Abraham's question to his father and people opens the same ancestral-idolatry dispute developed in the nearby verses.
The idols are tested for their ability to benefit or harm, undermining the practice inherited from the fathers.
The children of Adam are commanded not to worship Satan because he is a clear enemy.
They found their fathers astray and then hastened in their tracks, an exact statement of inherited following.
The followers are driven after their earlier forefathers on the same misguided course.
Followers in the Fire blame the leaders they followed and ask them to bear part of the punishment.
The challenge asks whether the people possess a book before this one to which they hold instead of revelation.
A recurring prophetic response meets the claim that fathers were found on a community and their tracks must be followed.
Whoever turns from the Merciful's reminder is assigned a Satan who becomes a close companion.
Satanic companions divert people from the path while the diverted think themselves guided.
The surrounding critique of inherited divine names begins by exposing an unauthorized division attributed to God.
Satan tells a person to disbelieve, then disowns him, and the outcome for both is the Fire.
The people insist that their inherited gods must not be abandoned, preserving ancestral idolatry by name.
Those ordered to reject false authorities instead seek their judgment, while Satan intends to lead them far astray.
Calling on false deities is identified as calling on a rebellious Satan.
Satan declares his program of leading people astray and commanding them to alter God's creation.
Obeying the majority is warned against because conjecture and guesswork lead away from God's path.
God's straight path is to be followed rather than divergent paths that separate people from His way.
Satan deceives Adam's children as he did their parents, warning them not to let him seduce them.
A person who abandons God's signs is followed by Satan and becomes one of the straying.
The addressees are told not to doubt the worship practiced by a people merely because their fathers practiced it before them.
Satan is permitted to entice with his voice and promises, an explicit picture of his active summons and deception.
Following the desire of one heedless of God's remembrance is forbidden, opposing unexamined allegiance.
Satan and his progeny are declared enemies, making their authority an invalid substitute for God.
Abraham asks his father why he worships what neither hears nor sees nor benefits him.
Abraham warns his father that Satanic obedience risks punishment from the Merciful.
Calling on what neither harms nor benefits is named manifest misguidance.
The one called besides God is nearer to harm than benefit, exposing the destructive direction of false invocation.
The fathers' worship of idols is brought under direct examination before their claimed benefit or harm is tested.
Worship besides God is called fabrication, while provision and worship are redirected exclusively to God.
People in the Fire say they obeyed their leaders and great ones, who led them from the way.
Those who disbelieve reject both this Qur'an and prior revelation, extending the refusal of revealed guidance.
Followers and leaders shift blame after following a plot that commanded disbelief and association with God.
Satan has already led many astray, followed by the rebuke that they should have used reason.
Those taking protectors besides God claim inherited-style mediators will bring them nearer to Him.
Evil companions make people's deeds attractive, leading them into a confirmed punishment.
After guidance is clear, turning back is attributed to Satan's enticement and false promises.
The question whether minds command evil addresses distorted moral authority without the focus's ancestry or invitation.
